block_05_direct_answer.title: Direct answer
block_05_direct_answer.body_html: Investor fit depends on whether the property matches the buyer’s actual investment objective. For Indian buyers, compare achievable rent, service charges, vacancy risk, future supply, holding costs, liquidity and likely buyer demand at resale. Stress-test weaker scenarios instead of relying on optimistic growth, yield or occupancy assumptions.

items.answer: Investor fit depends on whether the property matches the buyer’s actual investment objective. For Indian buyers, separate income, capital growth, preservation and exit goals so the property is tested against the outcome the buyer actually wants.
items.question: How should I assess whether a property suits an investor?

items.answer: Investment logic should connect the purchase price to realistic income, costs and exit options. Include purchase costs, financing, recurring charges, furnishing and likely operating expenses before comparing the economics of different options.
items.question: How should I assess the investment case?

items.answer: Rental demand should be checked through realistic tenant activity, not headline yield claims. Model periods without rent, tenant changes and leasing friction rather than assuming continuous occupancy throughout the holding period.
items.question: How should I assess rental demand?

items.answer: Resale potential depends on future buyer demand, competition and the property’s distinctiveness. Consider selling costs, financing appeal, expected marketing time and any contractual restrictions that could make an exit slower or more expensive.
items.question: How should I assess resale potential?

items.answer: A good exit strategy starts with understanding who could realistically buy the property later. Resale becomes fragile when only a very narrow audience is likely to value the property. Avoid relying on a single resale scenario, especially where the premium or future buyer pool is narrow.
